title: Inca Engineering
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · Unit 2 · Chapter 6 · Student Reader pp. 44–53
bigQuestion: How did the Inca use their engineering skills to manage and grow their empire?
note:
/* Every question, answer and excerpt below comes from the CKHG Grade 5 Unit 2
   Student Reader, Chapter 6 (pp. 44–53). Core Vocabulary for this chapter is
   official, engineer, mortar, suspension bridge and terrace — each is tested,
   and each question about one points at the sidebar box that defines it rather
   than at a sentence that merely uses the word. The sets follow the chapter's
   three reading segments, not equal page counts. */

sets.name: The Royal Road
sets.blurb: Two thousand miles of road, and the bridges that carried it over the gorges.

items.q: The chapter opens by comparing the Inca to the ancient Romans. What is the comparison?
opts: Both held an empire together by building roads across it
Both wrote down their laws and sent copies to every city
Both used horses and wagons to move an army quickly
Both built temples at the centre of every conquered town
items.why: It is one thing to conquer many lands, another to keep control of what you have conquered. The Romans built roads all across their empire. The Inca knew nothing of ancient Rome, but they too were great road builders.

items.q: What does official mean?
opts: A person who carries out a government duty
A soldier who has been promoted for bravery
Someone who designs a building or a road
A trader licensed to sell goods on the road
items.why: An official is a person who carries out a government duty. The roads made it possible for government officials to travel around the empire.

items.q: The reader gives three uses for the roads. Which does it call the most important?
opts: Letting the army travel quickly, to put down a rebellion
Letting government officials travel round the empire
Encouraging trade between one region and another
Giving travellers somewhere shaded to walk
items.why: The roads let officials travel and they encouraged trade. Most importantly, the roads allowed the army to travel quickly. This way, they could put down a rebellion or enforce the emperor's rule.

items.q: How long was the Royal Road, and how long did it hold its record?
opts: Over two thousand miles — the longest in the world until the 1800s
Over five hundred miles — the longest in the Americas at the time
Over four thousand miles — the longest until the railways came
Over one thousand miles — the longest until the Romans built theirs
items.why: Their Royal Road stretched over two thousand miles. It ran from the northern end of the empire to the southern tip. It was the longest road in the world until the 1800s.

items.q: What could a traveller find beside the Royal Road?
opts: Distance markers, shade trees, a canal, and storehouses with food
Inns run by the army where a bed could be paid for in gold
Toll gates where every trader had to declare what he carried
Watchtowers with a runner stationed in each one
items.why: Markers measured distances along the road. Trees shaded the road. A canal provided water for travelers. There were even roadside storehouses where travelers could get food at the end of the day.

items.q: What does mortar mean, and did the Inca use it?
opts: A cement-like material that hardens — no, they cut stone to fit
A tool for shaping stone — yes, on every paved stretch of road
A soft clay used for roofing — yes, on all of the storehouses
A rope made from plant fibre — no, they used leather instead
items.why: Mortar is a material used in building that is soft at first but then gets hard and rocklike. Modern builders use mortar to keep stones together. The Inca did not use any mortar. Instead, they cut stones so exactly that they fit together snugly.

sets.name: Bridges and Terraces
sets.blurb: A rope bridge that lasted five hundred years, and staircases cut into a mountain.

items.q: What did Inca builders not have?
opts: Earth-moving machinery, horses, oxen, or even the wheel
Stone tools, rope, or any way of measuring a distance
Enough workers to build anything larger than a bridge
Any way of crossing a river deeper than a stream
items.why: These builders had no earth-moving machinery. They did not have horses or oxen to pull wagons. They did not even have the wheel. Everything was done by hand. Yet the Inca were able to build roads so sturdy, not even heavy rains or flash floods could destroy them.

items.q: The reader compares the road network to a body. What is the comparison?
opts: The Royal Road was the spine, and the crossroads were nerves
The Royal Road was an artery, and the towns were the heart
The Royal Road was a backbone, and the bridges were joints
The Royal Road was a ribcage protecting the empire inside
items.why: At every valley, east-west roads crossed the Royal Road. The Royal Road was like the spine. The crossroads were like nerves branching out from it. This network of roads linked all parts of the empire together.

items.q: What does suspension bridge mean?
opts: One where the pathway hangs from ropes or cables
One built of stone arches resting on the riverbed
One that can be raised to let boats pass beneath
One made of logs laid flat across a narrow stream
items.why: A suspension bridge is a type of bridge in which the road or pathway hangs from ropes or cables that are attached to anchors or towers. The bridge over the Apurimac River was one.

items.q: How long was the bridge over the Apurimac River in service, and what kept it standing?
opts: From 1350 to 1890 — its ropes were replaced every two years
From 1350 to 1532 — it was rebuilt after every rainy season
From 1400 to 1700 — the stone piers were repaired each spring
From 1350 to 1450 — it was abandoned when the road moved
items.why: It was built over a steep river gorge in 1350. It was a suspension bridge, held together by heavy strands of rope. The ropes were replaced every two years. This amazing bridge was in service from 1350 until 1890 — more than five hundred years.

items.q: What does terrace mean?
opts: A flat piece of land carved out of a mountainside
A channel dug to carry water to a field that is dry
A wall built to hold back a river when it is in flood
A stone platform on which the harvest was left to dry
items.why: A terrace is a flat piece of land carved out of the side of a mountain or hill. The terraces created level fields that could be planted and harvested just like valley fields.

items.q: What two problems did farming on a mountainside cause, before the terraces?
opts: The incline made every task hard, and rain washed the crops out
The soil was frozen, and nothing but potatoes would grow in it
The fields were too far from the road to carry the harvest
The slopes were owned by the emperor and could not be farmed
items.why: Farming on a mountainside is challenging. The incline makes every task — plowing, planting, and harvesting — very difficult. In heavy downpours, water runs downhill and washes out crops. The Inca cut terraces into the sides of the mountains and built irrigation systems to bring water to them.

items.q: Put the problem and the Inca answer to it back in order.
steps: Crops have to be grown, but the empire is in the mountains.
On a slope, ploughing, planting and harvesting are all very difficult.
In heavy rain the water runs downhill and washes the crops out.
Terraces are cut into the mountainside to make level fields.
Irrigation systems are built to bring water to those fields.
items.why: The problem came first and the engineering answered it: level the ground by cutting terraces, then bring the water to it. The terraces created level fields that could be planted and harvested just like valley fields.

sets.name: Running an Empire Without Writing
sets.blurb: The quipu, the relay runners, Machu Picchu, and what happened to the conquered.

items.q: What problem did the Inca face in running their empire, and what was the quipu for?
opts: They had no writing — the quipu kept counts on knotted string
They had no calendar — the quipu tracked the days of the year
They had no coins — the quipu recorded what each family owed
They had no maps — the quipu showed where all the roads ran
items.why: The Inca had an advanced road system, but they had no written language. A quipu was a piece of string that had shorter strings of various colors dangling from it. By tying knots in a certain pattern, an official could record how many warriors were headed for a village or how much corn was in a storehouse.

items.q: How did an Inca messenger pass on his message?
opts: He memorised it and ran alongside the next runner to tell him
He carried a knotted string and handed it over at the station
He shouted it from the top of a hill to the next station
He rode a llama between the stations along the Royal Road
items.why: Since the Inca had no written language, these messengers did not carry a written note. Instead, a runner memorized his message and sprinted to a station, a mile or so away. Without slowing the pace, the second messenger ran alongside the first to hear the message, then continued on.

items.q: How fast was the relay, compared with the pony express riders of the 1860s?
opts: 150 miles a day on foot, against about 200 on horseback
50 miles a day on foot, against about 200 on horseback
300 miles a day on foot, against about 200 on horseback
150 miles a day on foot, against about 500 on horseback
items.why: A message could travel 150 miles in a day, so news could go from Quito to Cuzco in a little over a week. In the 1860s, the famous pony express riders of the American West were only able to cover about two hundred miles a day — and they rode on horseback.

items.q: Where is Machu Picchu, and what was it used for?
opts: A mountain fortress near Cuzco, a vacation spot for emperors
A port on the Pacific coast, the empire's main trading town
A fort on the northern border, built to watch for invaders
A farming village on the plateau, famous for its terraces
items.why: Machu Picchu is a mountain fortress seven thousand feet above sea level, located about fifty miles northwest of Cuzco. Archaeologists estimate it was built in the mid-1400s. For years it was a vacation spot for Inca emperors. Today it is the leading tourist attraction in Peru.

items.q: How did the Inca treat conquered people who cooperated?
opts: Few changes were made, and local gods could still be worshipped
They were moved at once to villages nearer to Cuzco
They were required to give up their language within a year
They were made to send their young men to Cuzco as sacrifices
items.why: When conquered people were cooperative, the Sapa Inca made few changes. Inca architects and managers oversaw the building of roads and temples, and the Inca taught their language and asked them to worship Inti. The worship of local gods was allowed, and sometimes those gods were even made a part of the Inca religion.

items.q: And what did the Sapa Inca do when conquered people were not cooperative?
opts: Moved troublemakers away, and settled loyal Inca among them
Destroyed their temples and forbade their language outright
Took their leaders hostage and held them in Cuzco
Left them alone but stopped the roads at their border
items.why: If conquered people were uncooperative, the Sapa Inca moved swiftly. He shipped troublemakers from their homes to villages where they were surrounded by local Inca citizens. He also shipped loyal Inca citizens to live among the conquered people.

items.q: How does the reader compare Inca and Aztec human sacrifice?
opts: It seems to have been less widespread among the Inca
It was far more widespread among the Inca
The two empires practised it in exactly the same way
The Inca did not practise it at all
items.why: Like the Aztec, the Inca built their empire by conquering other people, and they also sacrificed human beings for religious purposes. However, human sacrifice seems to have been less widespread in the Inca Empire. The Inca focused more on turning conquered people into loyal subjects.

build.q: Build the answer to the Big Question. Pick the two statements that best explain how engineering let the Inca manage and grow their empire.

tiles.t: Roads and bridges let officials, traders and above all the army move quickly across two thousand miles.
Terraces and irrigation turned mountainsides into level fields, so a mountain empire could feed itself.
They invented a written language and sent written orders along the roads.
They used horses and wagons to carry stone to the building sites.
They built Machu Picchu as the capital from which the empire was governed.
They used mortar to hold the paving stones of the Royal Road together.

build.answer: Holding a conquered land is harder than taking it. The Inca answer was engineering. The Royal Road and its bridges meant an army could reach a rebellion, officials could reach a village, and news could cross the empire in a week — all without the wheel, horses or oxen. And terraces cut into the Andes, watered by irrigation, meant a mountain empire could grow enough to feed twelve million people and fill the storehouses that kept them through a bad year.

why.title: The Royal Road
vocab: a person who carries out a government duty
text: It’s one thing to conquer many lands. It’s another thing to keep control of what you’ve conquered. Remember how the ancient Romans held their empire together? They built roads all across it.

The roads made it possible for government officials to travel around the empire. Roads also encouraged trade. Most importantly, the roads allowed the army to travel quickly. This way, they could put down a rebellion or enforce the emperor’s rule.

The Inca knew nothing of ancient Rome. But they too were great road builders. Their Royal Road stretched over two thousand miles. It ran from the northern end of the empire to the southern tip. It was the longest road in the world until the 1800s.

road.title: What the road was like
vocab: someone who uses science and math to design useful objects or buildings
text: The Royal Road was twenty-four feet wide in most places. Although it crossed mountains, valleys, deserts, and swamps, long stretches were straight as an arrow. Markers measured distances along the road. Trees shaded the road. A canal provided water for travelers. There were even roadside storehouses where travelers could get food at the end of the day.
Parts of the Royal Road were made of packed dirt. Other parts were paved. Inca engineers fitted paving stones together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle.

stone.title: Stone cut to fit
vocab: a material used in building that is soft at first but that then gets hard and rocklike
text: Modern builders use mortar, a cement-like material, to keep stones together. The Inca did not use any mortar. Instead, they cut stones so exactly that they fit together snugly.

The Royal Road shows the great skill of Inca builders. These builders had no earth-moving machinery. They did not have horses or oxen to pull wagons. They did not even have the wheel. Everything was done by hand. Yet the Inca were able to build roads so sturdy, not even heavy rains or flash floods could destroy them.

network.title: A spine and its nerves
text: The Royal Road was the main Inca road, but there were others. At every valley, east-west roads crossed the Royal Road. The Royal Road was like the spine. The crossroads were like nerves branching out from it. This network of roads linked all parts of the empire together.

bridge.title: Bridges Built for the Centuries
vocab: a type of bridge in which the road or pathway hangs from ropes or cables that are attached to anchors or towers
text: To build roads through mountains and across streams, the Inca had to build lots of bridges. Like the roads, these bridges are marvels of engineering. A bridge built over the Apurimac River in Peru is a fine example. It was built over a steep river gorge in 1350. It was a suspension bridge, held together by heavy strands of rope. The ropes were replaced every two years. This amazing bridge was in service from 1350 until 1890! For more than five hundred years, the bridge was maintained and used by the Inca.

terrace.title: Mountain Staircases
vocab: a flat piece of land carved out of the side of a mountain or hill
text: The Inca also used their engineering know-how to help them farm in the Andes. Farming on a mountainside is challenging. The incline makes every task—plowing, planting, and harvesting—very difficult. In heavy downpours, water runs downhill and washes out crops.

The Inca had to find a way to grow crops on the slopes of the Andes. Their solution was to cut terraces into the sides of the mountains. The terraces created level fields that could be planted and harvested just like valley fields. The Inca also built irrigation systems. This allowed them to bring water to the terraced fields.

quipu.title: Keeping It All Together
text: The Inca had an advanced road system, but they had no written language. How could they possibly run an empire of twelve million people that spanned the length of a continent without writing?

The Inca came up with some clever strategies. For instance, they invented a means for counting and record-keeping using a quipu. A quipu was a piece of string that had shorter strings of various colors dangling from it. By tying knots in a certain pattern on a quipu, an official could record how many warriors were headed for a village or how much corn was in a storehouse.

runner.title: The runners
text: The Inca also used messengers trained to run short distances to carry news. Since the Inca had no written language, these messengers did not carry a written note. Instead, a runner memorized his message and sprinted to a station, a mile or so away. There, the next runner would be waiting. Without slowing the pace, the second messenger ran alongside the first messenger to hear the message. Then the second messenger continued on.

The system was fast! A message could travel 150 miles in a day. This meant news could travel all the way from Quito to Cuzco in a little over a week. In the 1860s, the famous pony express riders of the American West were only able to cover about two hundred miles a day—and they rode on horseback!

machu.title: City in the Clouds
text: Another marvel of Inca engineering is the famous city of Machu Picchu. Machu Picchu is a mountain fortress seven thousand feet above sea level, located about fifty miles northwest of Cuzco. It sits in a high valley, between two peaks of the Andes.

Today, visitors can stand in the center of Machu Picchu. From there, they can see the ruins of an open plaza, a temple, and a place where archaeologists discovered Inca skeletons. The surrounding hillside is terraced for farming.
Archaeologists estimate that Machu Picchu was built in the mid-1400s. For years it was a vacation spot for Inca emperors. Today it is the leading tourist attraction in Peru.

conquered.title: Expanding the Empire
text: Like the Aztec, the Inca built their empire by conquering other people. They also sacrificed human beings for religious purposes. However, human sacrifice seems to have been less widespread in the Inca Empire. The Inca focused more on turning conquered people into loyal subjects.

When conquered people were cooperative, the Sapa Inca made few changes. Inca architects and managers went to new regions. Their job was to oversee the building of roads and temples. The Inca taught their language to the local people. They also asked them to worship the sun god Inti. The worship of local gods was allowed. Sometimes those gods were even made a part of the Inca religion.

If conquered people were uncooperative, the Sapa Inca moved swiftly. He shipped troublemakers from their homes to villages. There, they were surrounded by local Inca citizens. He also shipped loyal Inca citizens to live among the conquered people. In this way, the Sapa Inca was able to quickly build a large and unified empire.
